newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election turnout slackens to record low.
newsitem.headline: French election turnout slackens to record low.

text.p: Turnout in the first round of France's parliamentary election slackened to the lowest ever in late afternoon in a vote where President Jacques Chirac has gambled on the re-election of his conservative allies.

The Interior Ministry said turnout at 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) was 54.51 percent. That put it below the lowest previous score at the same time on a first round of a National Assembly vote of 54.7 percent in 1988.

Turnout in the first round of the 1988 parliamentary poll ended at 66.1 percent, the lowest since the start of the Fifth Republic in 1958. Sunday's turnout dipped after running at a relatively robust rate in early voting.

Opinion polls before a publication blackout a week ago showed the centre-right coalition led by Chirac's allies was likely to retain a majority in the 577-member National Assembly. A runoff will be held on June 1 in constituencies where no candidate wins the 50 percent needed to take a seat outright.

Low turnout might help Prime Minister Alain Juppe by cutting the number of three-way runoffs involving the far-right National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen, whose voters tend to opt for the centre-right if their candidate is eliminated.

Candidates need the support of 12.5 percent of all registered voters to reach the second-round runoffs. If turnout matches that of 1988, a candidate would need 19 percent of the votes cast to reach the second round.
